Tomato___Early_blight.description: Fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, creating dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves. Can reduce yield significantly if left untreated.
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves immediately and dispose properly
Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper
Improve air circulation by pruning and spacing plants
Apply organic mulch to prevent soil splash onto leaves
Water at the base of plants in the morning
prevention: Rotate crops - don't plant tomatoes in same spot for 3-4 years
Use disease-resistant varieties when available
Stake or cage plants for better air flow
Remove and destroy old plant debris at end of season
Avoid overhead watering
Apply preventive fungicide early in season
Maintain proper plant nutrition for strong immunity
organic_solutions: Baking soda spray: 1 tbsp baking soda + 1 tsp dish soap per gallon water
Neem oil application weekly during humid weather
Compost tea foliar spray for beneficial microbes
Copper fungicide (OMRI approved for organic gardening)
Milk spray: 1 part milk to 9 parts water
care_instructions: Monitor plants daily for new symptoms on lower leaves
Water deeply 1-2 inches per week, adjust based on rainfall
Apply balanced fertilizer (5-10-10) every 2-3 weeks
Mulch with 2-3 inches of organic material
Remove weeds that can harbor disease

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Devastating fungal disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. The same pathogen that caused the Irish Potato Famine. Can destroy entire crops within days in humid conditions.
treatment: Act immediately - this disease spreads extremely fast
Remove and destroy all infected plants (do NOT compost)
Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil or mancozeb every 5-7 days
Isolate affected area from healthy plants
Monitor all nearby tomato and potato plants closely
In severe cases, remove all plants in affected area
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (check your region's recommendations)
Ensure excellent air circulation between plants
Never work with plants when wet
Apply preventive fungicides before disease appears
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants
Monitor weather forecasts - late blight thrives in cool, wet conditions
Space plants wider than usual (3-4 feet apart)
organic_solutions: Unfortunately, organic controls are limited - focus on prevention
Consider growing in hoop houses or greenhouses for better control
care_instructions: ⚠️ URGENT: Check plants twice daily during humid weather
Remove any suspicious leaves immediately
Water only in morning to allow foliage to dry
Consider removing plants if disease is widespread
Alert neighboring gardeners if late blight is confirmed

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas species, creating small dark spots with yellow halos on leaves and fruit. Spreads rapidly in warm, wet conditions.
treatment: Remove and destroy severely infected plants
Apply copper-based bactericides at first sign
Reduce overhead watering immediately
Thin plants to improve air circulation
Disinfect tools between plants with 10% bleach solution
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Practice 3-4 year crop rotation
Avoid working with plants when wet
Space plants adequately (24-36 inches)
Use drip irrigation instead of sprinklers
Remove plant debris at end of season
Choose resistant varieties for your area
organic_solutions: Bacillus subtilis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens products
care_instructions: Water at soil level only, never wet foliage
Monitor plants during warm, humid periods
Maintain plant vigor with proper nutrition
Sanitize tools after each use
Avoid handling plants when wet from dew or rain

Apple___Apple_scab.description: Fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis, creating olive-green to brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Most severe in areas with cool, wet springs.
treatment: Rake and destroy all fallen leaves (primary infection source)
Apply fungicides from green tip through petal fall
Prune to improve air circulation and light penetration
Remove severely infected fruit and twigs
Continue fungicide applications through June in wet years
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties (Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise)
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Maintain 20-30 foot spacing between trees
Prune trees annually to improve air flow
Apply dormant oil spray in early spring
Mulch with wood chips (not leaves)
Monitor weather for infection periods
organic_solutions: Baking soda spray (5 tbsp per gallon)
Remove leaf litter to break disease cycle
care_instructions: Scout trees weekly during spring for first symptoms
Water at tree base, avoid wetting foliage
Apply balanced fertilizer in early spring
Thin fruit to prevent overcrowding
Maintain proper tree structure through pruning

Pepper___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease causing leaf spots and fruit lesions on pepper plants. Can significantly reduce yield and fruit quality.
treatment: Remove infected leaves and destroy them
Apply copper bactericides weekly
Avoid overhead irrigation
Increase spacing between plants if possible
Disinfect pruning tools between plants
prevention: Start with certified disease-free seeds
Rotate peppers with non-solanaceous crops
Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses
Avoid working in garden when plants are wet
Space plants 18-24 inches apart
Choose resistant varieties when available
organic_solutions: Remove and destroy infected plant material
care_instructions: Inspect plants regularly, especially after rain
Water early in the day at soil level
Maintain consistent soil moisture
Fertilize with balanced organic fertilizer
Mulch to prevent soil splash
